title: The Eye That Sees Upside Down
blurb: Every picture that lands inside your eye is upside down and backwards, and there is a hole in your vision you have never noticed.

blocks.text: You have two eyes. Your eyes let you see. Look in a mirror. See the white part. See the ring of color. That ring can be brown or blue or green or gray. meta.templateLabel: The Eye That Sees Upside Down

notes: The pupil is a hole, not a dot
The iris is a tiny muscle
Blue eyes have no blue in them

blocks.prompt: The Hole in the Middle of Your Eye
blocks.text: Look at the black dot in the middle of your eye. It is not a dot. It is a hole. The hole is called the pupil. Light goes through it, and that is how you see. The ring of color around it is called the iris. The iris is a tiny muscle. In a dark room, the iris opens the hole wide to let more light in. In bright sun, the iris closes it small. Ask someone to look at your eyes in the dark, then turn on the light. Watch the hole shrink. Your eyes fix themselves, and you never even feel it.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.
items: What is the black dot in your eye really?
What is the ring of color called?
What does the iris do in a dark room?
answers: it is a hole called the pupil
the iris
it opens the pupil wide to let more light in

answers: pupil
iris

small

3.title: The Eye That Sees Upside Down
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

meta.templateLabel: The Eye That Sees Upside Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: The lens is about the size of a pea
The picture inside your eye is upside down

blocks.prompt: Your Eye Is a Camera
blocks.text: Your eye is built almost exactly like a camera. Light bounces off everything around you. Some of that light comes toward your face and hits the clear window at the front of your eye. It passes through the pupil, which is just a hole. Behind the hole sits a lens, soft and clear and about the size of a pea. The lens bends the light and aims it at the back wall of your eye. That back wall is called the retina. It is thin, and it is covered in millions of tiny cells that notice light. When light lands on them, they send a message down a thick nerve to your brain. Here is the strange part. The lens flips the picture over on the way through. Every image that lands on your retina is upside down and backwards. Your brain turns it the right way up so fast that you have never once noticed. You are not really seeing with your eyes. You are seeing with your brain, and your eyes just deliver the mail.

4.title: The Eye That Sees Upside Down
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Eye That Sees Upside Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 120 million rods, about 6 million cones
One rod can catch a single particle of light
Rods see no color at all
Sharp vision comes from a patch the size of a pinhead
Look slightly to one side to see a faint star better

blocks.prompt: Two Kinds of Light Catchers
blocks.text: The back of your eye is lined with a thin sheet called the retina, and packed into it are more than a hundred million cells whose only job is to catch light. They are not all the same. They come in two kinds, and the difference explains almost everything strange about how you see. The first kind is called a rod. You have roughly 120 million of them, and they are extraordinarily sensitive. A rod can react to a single particle of light. But rods are colorblind. They report brightness and nothing else. They are also spread mostly around the edges of the retina, away from the center. The second kind is called a cone. You only have about 6 million, they need far more light to fire, and they come in three types, each tuned to a different range of color. Cones are crowded into one tiny patch at the center of the retina, roughly the size of a pinhead. That patch is the only place you see sharp detail. Now the strange parts make sense. At night the world goes gray, because your cones have shut down and only your rods are left working, and rods do not do color. Out of the corner of your eye things look blurry, because there are almost no cones out there. And a faint star will vanish if you stare straight at it, then reappear when you look slightly to one side. You are moving its light off your cones and onto your sensitive rods.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: In your own words, what is the main difference between a rod and a cone?
Why does the world lose its color at night?
The passage says a faint star vanishes when you look straight at it. Explain why, using what you know about the retina.
You have twenty times more rods than cones. Why do you think your sharpest vision still comes from the cones?
answers: rods catch dim light but see no color; cones need bright light and see color and detail
cones need bright light, so at night only the colorblind rods are still working
(inference: staring puts its light on the cone patch, which is not sensitive enough for a faint star)
(inference: the cones are packed tightly into the one patch built for detail, and rods only report brightness)

5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Eye That Sees Upside Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About one million nerve fibers leave each eye
The blind spot is where the optic nerve exits
Your eyes jump three to four times a second
Your brain deletes the blur during each jump
Two eyes together cover each other's blind spot

blocks.prompt: The Hole You Cannot See
blocks.text: There is a hole in your vision right now. It is roughly the size of a lemon held at arm's length, it sits a little to the outside of where you are looking, and you have never seen it. You cannot see it. That is the whole problem. The hole is called the blind spot, and it exists for a plain mechanical reason. Every one of the roughly one million nerve fibers leaving your retina has to get out of your eyeball somehow, so they bundle together and punch through the retina in one place, forming the optic nerve. At that exit wound there is no room for light cells. Light landing there is simply not recorded. Each eye has one. You would expect to notice a hole. You do not, and the reason is more interesting than the hole. Your brain does not receive a picture from your eye and look at it. Your brain builds a picture, and it builds it out of whatever it can get: the good data from the rest of the retina, the matching view from your other eye, the pattern it expects to be there, and its memory of a fraction of a second ago. Where data is missing, the brain fills the gap with its best guess and hands you the result without mentioning the edit. It does this constantly. Your eyes are not gliding smoothly across this page. They are jerking, three or four times a second, in fast jumps called saccades, and during each jump the image smears into uselessness. Your brain throws that smear away and stitches the still frames together. You are watching a film with most of the frames deleted and the gaps invented, and it looks seamless. So the honest description is this. You do not see the world. You see your brain's running model of the world, corrected against your eyes several times a second. It is usually right, which is why the illusion holds.

6.title: The Eye That Sees Upside Down
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Eye That Sees Upside Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Vertebrate photoreceptors point away from the light
The optic nerve punches through the retina, making the blind spot
Octopus retinas face the light and have no blind spot
The vertebrate eye grows out of brain tissue
Muller cells guide light through the retina like fiber optics
About one million nerve fibers per optic nerve

blocks.prompt: The Eye Is Built Backwards, and It Works Anyway
blocks.text: Here is a fact that sounds like a mistake. Your retina is installed backwards. Think about what a retina is for. It is a sheet of cells at the back of the eye whose entire job is to catch light. You would assume, then, that the light-catching ends of those cells point toward the incoming light. In your eye, they do not. They point the other way, toward the back of your head. The wiring, the blood vessels, and several layers of supporting nerve cells all sit in front of the photoreceptors, and every particle of light that reaches a rod or a cone has to travel through that tangle first. The consequences are real. Because the nerve fibers are on the wrong side, they must eventually gather up and drill a hole straight through the retina to escape the eyeball. That hole is the blind spot, and you have one in each eye. Because the retina is layered rather than anchored, it can peel away from the wall behind it, which is what a detached retina is. Now consider an octopus. An octopus eye looks remarkably like yours: a cornea, an iris, a lens, a retina. It evolved completely separately, hundreds of millions of years down a different branch, which makes it one of the best examples of convergent evolution we have. And the octopus retina faces the right way. Its photoreceptors point at the light. Its nerve fibers exit from behind. An octopus has no blind spot. So why are you the one with the design flaw? The answer is not that vertebrate eyes are worse. It is that evolution cannot start over. The vertebrate eye grew outward from developing brain tissue, and the cephalopod eye folded inward from skin. Both lineages were then stuck improving whatever they had already committed to. Evolution has no draft stage. It can only renovate. And here is the twist. The backwards layout turns out to carry advantages nobody designed. Photoreceptors are among the hungriest cells in the body, and sitting at the back places them directly against the choroid, a dense bed of blood vessels that feeds them and carries away heat. Behind them lies the retinal pigment epithelium, a dark layer that recycles worn-out light-sensitive molecules and absorbs stray light that would otherwise scatter and blur the image. And the tangle in front is less of an obstacle than it appears. Long, thin Muller cells run through the retina like fiber optic cables, funneling light past the clutter and delivering it to the photoreceptors below. The octopus, meanwhile, has a clean retina and only one type of photoreceptor. It is very probably colorblind. The lesson is not that your eye is badly made or beautifully made. It is that living things are not made at all. They are inherited, patched, and repurposed, and what looks like a flaw is usually just history you can still see.
